claims.claim: The basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between Vibrio and E. coli.
claims.source: Because each of the SecA (Kunioka et al., 1998), SecY (Bhattacharyya and Das, 1997), SecE (Nishiyama et al., 1998) and the two SecD/F (Ishii et al., 2015) homologs of Vibrio can function in E. coli cells, the basic structure and function of the Sec machinery and the interaction modes among these factors should be well conserved between these species.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the functional complementation of Vibrio Sec components in E. coli.

claims.claim: VemP(W124pBPA) generates a crosslink of ~30 kDa that is immunoprecipitable with an anti-uL22 antibody.
claims.source: An XL of ~30 kDa, observed for the VemP(W124pBPA) variant, was immunoprecipitatable with an anti-uL22 antibody (Figure 1B, right).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking and immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1B.

claims.claim: Trp-124 of VemP is positioned close to the ribosomal protein uL22 in vivo.
claims.source: The proximity of Trp-124 to uL22 in vivo is consistent with a recent cryo-EM study showing that Trp-124 of arrested VemP is positioned close to the ribosomal protein uL22 (Figure 1B, left) (Su et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: The in vivo crosslinking data is consistent with the cryo-EM structure, supported by citation to Su et al., 2017.

claims.claim: VemP(F81pBPA) and VemP(T83pBPA) generate crosslinks of ~25 kDa that contain SecG.
claims.source: VemP(F81pBPA) and VemP(T83pBPA) generated XLs of ~25 kDa. We envisioned that the crosslinked partner could either be SecE (~14 kDa) or SecG (~12 kDa), small components of the translocon, because VemP engages in the Sec-dependent translocation (Mori et al., 2018). We reasoned that these XLs contained SecG because they reacted with an anti-SecG antibody (Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A) and disappeared in the ΔsecG strain (VemP(F81pBPA); Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking, immunoprecipitation, and genetic experiments shown in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 3A.

claims.claim: VemP derivatives having pBPA in a middle region (Arg-74, Asp-76, Leu-78, Asn-82, and Trp-86) generate crosslinks with SecY.
claims.source: To investigate possible crosslinking with SecY, the main component of the translocon, we used a host strain having a chromosomal secY-his10 gene. We detected the SecYxVemP XLs for the VemP derivatives having pBPA in a middle region (Arg-74, Asp-76, Leu-78, Asn-82, and Trp-86) of VemP among materials pulled-down by polyhistidine affinity isolation (Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking and His-tag affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 4A.

claims.claim: VemP interacts with Ffh through its signal sequence (Ala-15 position).
claims.source: We found that VemP also interacts with SRP through the PiXie analysis using a strain carrying chromosomal ffh-his10. Placement of pBPA within the signal sequence (Ala-15 position) allowed for the generation of a VemPxFfh XL that was His-tag affinity isolated (Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking and His-tag affinity purification experiments shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 4B.

claims.claim: PpiD interacts with the VemP region (Tyr-36 to Ser-60) that follows the periplasmic end of the signal sequence.
claims.source: We addressed the possibility of their involvement using their His-tagged derivatives and found that a XL was His-tag affinity-isolated when a cell with chromosomal ppiD-his10 was used (Figure 1F), but not with the other his10 constructs (Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D). Furthermore, the XL was immunoprecipitated with an anti-PpiD antibody and were not generated in a ΔppiD cell (Figure 1—figure supplement 3B). These results indicate that PpiD interacts with the VemP region (Tyr-36 to Ser-60) that follows the periplasmic end of the signal sequence.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking, His-tag affinity purification, immunoprecipitation, and genetic experiments shown in Figure 1F, Figure 1—figure supplement 3B, and Figure 1—figure supplement 4C,D.

claims.claim: None of the VemP crosslinks with uL22, Ffh, SecG, SecY, and PpiD were immunoprecipitated with the anti-FLAG antibody, indicating that the VemP component in these crosslinks lacks the C-terminal tag and are in the elongation-arrested state.
claims.source: None of the VemP XLs with uL22, Ffh, SecG, SecY, and PpiD described above were immunoprecipitated with the anti-FLAG antibody (Figure 1—figure supplement 5), indicating that the VemP component in these XLs lacks the C-terminal tag and, therefore, are in the elongation-arrested state.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunoprecipitation experiments shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 5.

claims.claim: The uL22- and Ffh-crosslinks decreased slightly faster than the arrested VemP during the chase period.
claims.source: While the decrease rates of the SecG-XLs and the arrested VemP were almost the same, the uL22- and Ffh-XLs decreased slightly faster than the arrested VemP (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by kinetic analysis of crosslinks during pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The decrease rates of the SecG-crosslinks and the arrested VemP were almost the same.
claims.source: While the decrease rates of the SecG-XLs and the arrested VemP were almost the same, the uL22- and Ffh-XLs decreased slightly faster than the arrested VemP (Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by kinetic analysis of crosslinks during pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2B,C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: Ffh (SRP) and uL22 interact with the arrested VemP polypeptide before targeting to the translocon.
claims.source: These results suggest that Ffh (SRP) and uL22 interact with the arrested VemP polypeptide before targeting to the translocon, in agreement with their cellular functions and localization.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that uL22- and Ffh-crosslinks decrease faster than arrested VemP, and consistent with their known cellular functions.

claims.claim: NaN3 treatment of cells causes the stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP in living cells.
claims.source: This was verified by examining the effect of NaN3, a SecA inhibitor, on the VemP-crosslinkings. NaN3 treatment of cells causes the stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP in living cells (Mori et al., 2018), suggesting that inhibition of SecA prevents VemP from initiating its translocation into the translocon.
claims.evidence: This is established knowledge from previous work by the authors, supported by citation to Mori et al., 2018.

claims.claim: Inhibition of SecA prevents VemP from initiating its translocation into the translocon.
claims.source: NaN3 treatment of cells causes the stabilization of the AP-un form of VemP in living cells (Mori et al., 2018), suggesting that inhibition of SecA prevents VemP from initiating its translocation into the translocon. We confirmed it by pulse-chase experiments using a secA51 (Ts) mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Inferred from the stabilization of AP-un form upon NaN3 treatment and confirmed by experiments with secA51(Ts) mutant shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: The arrest cancelation of VemP was severely and specifically retarded at high temperature in the secA51(Ts) mutant cells.
claims.source: We confirmed it by pulse-chase experiments using a secA51 (Ts) mutant cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 3). As expected, the arrest cancelation of VemP was severely and specifically retarded at high temperature in the secA51(Ts) mutant cells, but not in its isogenic wild type cells.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3.

claims.claim: NaN3 treatment increased the VemP crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh.
claims.source: We found that the NaN3 treatment increased the VemP crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh, but decreased its crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking experiments with NaN3 treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B.

claims.claim: NaN3 treatment decreased VemP crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD.
claims.source: We found that the NaN3 treatment increased the VemP crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh, but decreased its crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD (Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by photo-crosslinking experiments with NaN3 treatment shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4A,B.

claims.claim: The arrested VemP interacts with SRP and uL22 before the interactions with the translocon and PpiD on the membrane.
claims.source: These results suggest that the arrested VemP interacts with SRP and uL22 before the interactions with the translocon and PpiD on the membrane.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the NaN3 treatment experiments showing increased crosslinking with uL22 and Ffh but decreased crosslinking with SecY, SecG, and PpiD.

claims.claim: The PpiD-crosslinks tended to decrease more slowly than SecG-crosslinks or the arrested VemP.
claims.source: In contrast to the uL22- and Ffh-XLs, the PpiD-XLs tended to decrease more slowly than SecG-XLs or the arrested VemP (Figure 2B,C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by kinetic analysis of crosslinks during pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 2B,C.

claims.claim: VemP is recognized by PpiD after it engages with the translocon.
claims.source: This suggests that VemP is recognized by PpiD after it engages with the translocon, being consistent with the topology of PpiD that has a functional domain in the periplasm.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the kinetic analysis showing that PpiD-crosslinks decrease more slowly than SecG-crosslinks, and consistent with the known topology of PpiD.

claims.claim: The Ffh-depletion upon removal of arabinose from the medium stabilized the AP-un form of VemP.
claims.source: The Ffh-depletion upon removal of arabinose from the medium stabilized the AP-un form of VemP (Figure 3A), indicating an impairment of the targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments using Ffh-depletable strain shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Ffh-depletion impairs the targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon.
claims.source: The Ffh-depletion upon removal of arabinose from the medium stabilized the AP-un form of VemP (Figure 3A), indicating an impairment of the targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the stabilization of AP-un form upon Ffh-depletion shown in Figure 3A.

claims.claim: Deletion of the secB gene severely compromised export of MBP, a SecB-dependent substrate.
claims.source: Consistent with the observation, deletion of the secB gene that encodes a secretion-specific chaperone severely compromised export of MBP, a SecB-dependent substrate, but exhibited the normal arrest cancelation of VemP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the co-translational targeting of a VemP-ribosome complex.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments using ΔsecB strain shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: Deletion of the secB gene exhibited the normal arrest cancelation of VemP.
claims.source: Consistent with the observation, deletion of the secB gene that encodes a secretion-specific chaperone severely compromised export of MBP, a SecB-dependent substrate, but exhibited the normal arrest cancelation of VemP (Figure 3—figure supplement 1), supporting the co-translational targeting of a VemP-ribosome complex.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments using ΔsecB strain shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claims.claim: The synthesis of V.SecD2 was elevated under the Ffh-depleted conditions in E. coli cells carrying a vemP-V.secD2/F2 plasmid.
claims.source: To verify this point, we examined the V.SecD2 expression in WAM121 cells carrying a vemP-V.secD2/F2 plasmid, and found that the synthesis of V.SecD2 was indeed elevated under the Ffh-depleted conditions (Figure 3B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 3B.

claims.claim: In the Ffh-depletable strain of V. alginolyticus, the V.SecD2 expression was induced in the arabinose-free medium even in the presence of a sufficient level of Na+.
claims.source: We also examined the effect of an Ffh-depletion on the V.SecD2 expression in the cognate organism, V. alginolyticus (Figure 3C). Under a Na+-rich growth condition, the Na+-driven V.SecD1/F1 in this organism was fully functional, leading to the efficient arrest cancelation of VemP and consequent tight repression of V.SecD2 (Ishii et al., 2015). In the Ffh-depletable strain of V. alginolyticus with the arabinose promoter-controlled ffh, the V.SecD2 expression was induced in the arabinose-free medium even in the presence of a sufficient level of Na+, consistent with the notion that the Ffh-depletion compromises the targeting of VemP and stabilizes its translation arrest.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 3C.

claims.claim: SRP is crucial for the translocon targeting of VemP, which is a prerequisite for the proper regulation of the V.SecD2/F2 expression in Vibrio.
claims.source: These results suggest that SRP is crucial for the translocon targeting of VemP, which is a prerequisite for the proper regulation of the V.SecD2/F2 expression in Vibrio.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that Ffh-depletion stabilizes VemP arrest and induces V.SecD2 expression in both E. coli and V. alginolyticus.

claims.claim: VemP was kept in the arrested state much more stably in the ΔppiD cells than in the ppiD+ E. coli cells.
claims.source: Pulse-chase analysis showed that VemP was kept in the arrested state much more stably in the ΔppiD cells than in the ppiD+ E. coli cells (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: Translocation of MBP was retarded by the ppiD disruption, albeit less pronouncedly than VemP.
claims.source: We note that translocation of a secretory protein MBP (maltose-binding protein) was also retarded by the ppiD disruption, albeit less pronouncedly (Figure 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4A.

claims.claim: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in E. coli.
claims.source: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in E. coli (Figure 4B) and in Vibrio (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 4B.

claims.claim: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in Vibrio.
claims.source: The loss of ppiD increased the V.SecD2 expression in E. coli (Figure 4B) and in Vibrio (Figure 4C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claims.claim: PpiD plays a crucial role in the arrest-cancelation of VemP.
claims.source: These results show that PpiD plays a crucial role in the arrest-cancelation of VemP.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that ppiD disruption stabilizes VemP arrest and induces V.SecD2 expression.

claims.claim: The PpiD disruption caused an accumulation of the AP-pro form of VemP.
claims.source: The PpiD disruption caused an accumulation of the AP-pro form of VemP in contrast to the Ffh depletion that led to the AP-un accumulation (compare Figures 3A and 4A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by comparing pulse-chase experiments shown in Figures 3A and 4A.

claims.claim: PpiD acts on the periplasmic side after the signal sequence cleavage of the arrested VemP.
claims.source: These results support the notion that PpiD acts on the periplasmic side after the signal sequence cleavage of the arrested VemP, whereas Ffh acts earlier on the cytosolic side.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that PpiD disruption causes accumulation of AP-pro form while Ffh depletion causes accumulation of AP-un form.

claims.claim: Ffh acts earlier on the cytosolic side compared to PpiD.
claims.source: These results support the notion that PpiD acts on the periplasmic side after the signal sequence cleavage of the arrested VemP, whereas Ffh acts earlier on the cytosolic side.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that Ffh depletion causes accumulation of AP-un form while PpiD disruption causes accumulation of AP-pro form.

claims.claim: The overproduction of SecD/F facilitated the arrest cancelation in wild type cells.
claims.source: The role of SecD/F itself in the VemP arrest cancelation can be seen from the prolonged VemP arrest in the secD1 (a mutation causing SecD/F depletion) E. coli cells (Figure 4D, vector lanes) and the enhanced arrest cancelation by overproduction of SecD/F (Figure 4D, left, vector vs. secD/F).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The arrested state of VemP was stabilized in the ΔppiD cells.
claims.source: The arrested state of VemP was stabilized in the ΔppiD cells (Figure 4D, vector lanes), showing that its function is required for the active translocation and the arrest cancelation of VemP.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: The overproduction of PpiD facilitated the arrest cancelation in wild type cells.
claims.source: Whereas the overproduction of PpiD facilitated the arrest cancelation, as expected, SecD/F's overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the ppiD defect.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: SecD/F's overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the ppiD defect.
claims.source: Whereas the overproduction of PpiD facilitated the arrest cancelation, as expected, SecD/F's overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the ppiD defect.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: PpiD overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the secD1 mutation.
claims.source: Conversely, PpiD overproduction was ineffective in relieving the arrested state due to the secD1 mutation (Figure 4D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 4D.

claims.claim: Both SecD/F and PpiD are specifically required for the cancelation of VemP arrest.
claims.source: These results rule out the possibility that the roles of SecD/F and PpiD in arrest cancelation are redundant. Instead, both of them are specifically required for the cancelation of VemP arrest, raising the possibility that they interact with each other.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the genetic complementation experiments showing that overproduction of either factor alone cannot rescue the defect caused by loss of the other.

claims.claim: When pBPA was incorporated into the position of Asp-359 in the P1 head of SecD, its crosslinks with PpiD were detected.
claims.source: We then studied this point by in vivo photo-crosslinking. When pBPA was incorporated into the position of Asp-359 in the P1 head of SecD, its XLs with PpiD were detected (Figure 4E).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by in vivo photo-crosslinking experiments shown in Figure 4E.

claims.claim: PpiD resides in close proximity to the mobile P1 head of SecD of the VemP-translocating translocon.
claims.source: Thus, PpiD resides in close proximity to the mobile P1 head of SecD of the VemP-translocating translocon.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the crosslinking of pBPA at position 359 in SecD with PpiD.

claims.claim: Incorporation of pBPA to some VemP residues compromised the translation arrest of VemP.
claims.source: Our systematic pBPA scanning incidentally revealed that incorporation of this amino acid analog to some VemP residues compromised the translation arrest of VemP (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by systematic pBPA scanning shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claims.claim: Trp substitutions at several residues destabilized the translation arrest in similar ways to the corresponding pBPA substitutions.
claims.source: We selected several residues among them (shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), and replaced them individually with Trp (having a bulky, hydrophobic side chain like pBPA). The Trp substitutions destabilized the translation arrest in similar ways to the corresponding pBPA substitutions.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: The R85W mutation had the strongest effect in destabilizing the translation arrest among the tested mutations.
claims.source: Among them, the R85W mutation had the strongest effect; it decreased the ratio of arrested forms to total VemP to the level comparable with that observed with a previously identified arrest motif mutation, W143A (Mori et al., 2018).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claims.claim: Several other replacements of Arg-85 by residues of different properties also impaired apparently the translation arrest of VemP.
claims.source: Several other replacements of Arg-85 by residues of different properties also impaired apparently the translation arrest of VemP (Figure 5A).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments shown in Figure 5A.

claims.claim: The R85W mutation abrogated the arrest-mediated up-regulation of V.secD2.
claims.source: The R85W mutation abrogated the arrest-mediated up-regulation of V.secD2 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-labeling experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claims.claim: Arg-85 is crucial for the stable translation arrest of VemP in vivo.
claims.source: These results showed that Arg-85 is crucial for the stable translation arrest of VemP in vivo.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the mutagenesis experiments showing that mutations at Arg-85 destabilize the translation arrest and abrogate arrest-mediated regulation.

claims.claim: The R85W mutation did not exert a negative effect on the arrest in the secretion-impaired cell.
claims.source: In the Sec-deficient cells (see Materials and methods), the arrested form of WT VemP was stabilized (Mori et al., 2018), while that of VemP(W143A) was rapidly converted to the full-length form (Figure 5B). In contrast, the R85W mutant did not exert a negative effect on the arrest in the secretion-impaired cell (Figure 5B).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments in Sec-deficient cells shown in Figure 5B.

claims.claim: The R85 mutation did not affect the elongation arrest in the absence of the signal sequence.
claims.source: As another means to render VemP indifferent to secretion, we deleted its signal sequence. The R85 mutation did not affect the elongation arrest in the absence of the signal sequence. By sharp contrast, the W143A mutation abolished the arrest even in the absence of the signal sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments using VemP lacking signal sequence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The W143A mutation abolished the arrest even in the absence of the signal sequence.
claims.source: As another means to render VemP indifferent to secretion, we deleted its signal sequence. The R85 mutation did not affect the elongation arrest in the absence of the signal sequence. By sharp contrast, the W143A mutation abolished the arrest even in the absence of the signal sequence (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by immunoblotting experiments using VemP lacking signal sequence shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claims.claim: The mode of involvement of Arg-85 in the elongation arrest is fundamentally different from that of Trp-143.
claims.source: Thus, the mode of involvement of Arg-85 in the elongation arrest is fundamentally different from that of Trp-143.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of R85 and W143A mutations under secretion-deficient conditions and in the absence of signal sequence.

claims.claim: Arg-85 acts after targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon, probably during its translocation.
claims.source: These data revealed that Arg-85 acts after targeting of the VemP-ribosome complex to the translocon, probably during its translocation.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the observation that R85 mutations only affect arrest under secretion-proficient conditions.

claims.claim: The R85W mutation allows the efficient translocation of VemP even in the absence of PpiD.
claims.source: In the ΔppiD strain, while a significant fraction of the VemP(W143A) was retained in the arrested forms, the VemP(R85W/W143A) double mutant was almost completely translocated to generate the mature (processed) FL form. The results suggest that the R85W mutation allows the efficient translocation of VemP even in the absence of PpiD, indicating that the mutation at Arg-85 reduces PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: The mutation at Arg-85 reduces PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
claims.source: In the ΔppiD strain, while a significant fraction of the VemP(W143A) was retained in the arrested forms, the VemP(R85W/W143A) double mutant was almost completely translocated to generate the mature (processed) FL form. The results suggest that the R85W mutation allows the efficient translocation of VemP even in the absence of PpiD, indicating that the mutation at Arg-85 reduces PpiD-dependency of the VemP translocation.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claims.claim: A small but significant amount of the full-length precursor form of VemP(F.S.) was observed in the ΔppiD strain, suggesting the translocation of VemP(F.S.) depends on PpiD.
claims.source: As expected, the VemP(F.S.) derivative no longer underwent the elongation arrest even in the ΔppiD strain. We observed a small but significant amount of the full-length precursor form of VemP(F.S.) in the ΔppiD strain, suggesting the translocation of VemP(F.S.) depends on PpiD.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The additional introduction of the R85W mutation into VemP(F.S.) greatly reduced the amount of the precursor.
claims.source: Interestingly, the additional introduction of the R85W mutation into VemP(F.S.) greatly reduced the amount of the precursor.
claims.evidence: Demonstrated by pulse-chase experiments shown in Figure 5C.

claims.claim: The Arg-85 residue somehow retards the translocation of VemP independently of its translation arrest.
claims.source: These results indicate that while the Arg-85 residue somehow retards the translocation of VemP independently of its translation arrest, it is released by the function of PpiD; in other words, Arg-85 imposes PpiD-dependency on the translocation of VemP.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that R85W mutation reduces PpiD-dependency even in the absence of translation arrest.

claims.claim: Arg-85 imposes PpiD-dependency on the translocation of VemP.
claims.source: These results indicate that while the Arg-85 residue somehow retards the translocation of VemP independently of its translation arrest, it is released by the function of PpiD; in other words, Arg-85 imposes PpiD-dependency on the translocation of VemP.
claims.evidence: Inferred from the experiments showing that R85W mutation reduces PpiD-dependency of VemP translocation.

claims.claim: The function of Arg-85 could repress the arrest cancelation of VemP until translocation of VemP proceeds to an appropriate stage, at which PpiD and SecD/F come in to enhance the late stage of translocation.
claims.source: The function of Arg-85 could repress the arrest cancelation of VemP until translocation of VemP proceeds to an appropriate stage, at which PpiD and SecD/F come in to enhance the late stage of translocation.
claims.evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the experimental results regarding Arg-85 function.

claims.claim: In the cytosol, SRP recognizes and binds to the signal sequence of VemP and targets the nascent chain to the translocon.
claims.source: (i) In the cytosol, SRP recognizes and binds to the signal sequence of VemP and targets the nascent chain to the translocon. During this co-translational targeting step, the ongoing translation of VemP is subject to elongation arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing SRP interaction with VemP signal sequence and its requirement for membrane targeting.

claims.claim: During the co-translational targeting step, the ongoing translation of VemP is subject to elongation arrest.
claims.source: (i) In the cytosol, SRP recognizes and binds to the signal sequence of VemP and targets the nascent chain to the translocon. During this co-translational targeting step, the ongoing translation of VemP is subject to elongation arrest.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing that VemP undergoes translation arrest.

claims.claim: The signal sequence of VemP is inserted into the lateral gate region while the mature region of VemP is going to span the translocon's polypeptide-conducting channel.
claims.source: (ii) The signal sequence is then inserted into the lateral gate region while the mature region of VemP is going to span the translocon's polypeptide-conducting channel.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing VemP interaction with the translocon.

claims.claim: The early step of translocation is facilitated by the SecA ATPase and accompanied by the signal sequence cleavage.
claims.source: This early step of translocation is facilitated by the SecA ATPase (Figure 2—figure supplement 3) and accompanied by the signal sequence cleavage.
claims.evidence: This is a proposed model based on the experimental data showing SecA requirement and signal sequence processing.

claims.claim: The inhibition of SecA with NaN3 causes accumulation of the AP-un form of VemP.
claims.source: Therefore, the inhibition of SecA with NaN3 causes accumulation of the AP-un form of VemP.
claims.evidence: This is inferred from the experimental data showing that NaN3 treatment stabilizes the AP-un form.

claims.claim: SecD/F and PpiD interact with VemP and cooperate in canceling the translation arrest of VemP while aiding its further translocation.

results.result: SRP (Ffh) is required for membrane-targeting of VemP nascent chains. VemP interacts with Ffh through its signal sequence (position Ala-15), and Ffh-depletion stabilizes the unprocessed arrested form (AP-un) and induces V.SecD2 expression in both E. coli and V. alginolyticus.
results.evaluation: Claims C2, C4, C54, C68-C69, and C72-C74 collectively demonstrate SRP's role through multiple complementary approaches: photo-crosslinking identifies the interaction site (C54), depletion experiments show functional requirement (C68-C69), and downstream effects on V.SecD2 expression validate physiological significance in both heterologous and native systems (C72-C73). The convergence of structural, functional, and regulatory evidence strongly supports this result.

results.result: PpiD cooperates with SecD/F in VemP translocation and arrest-cancelation. PpiD interacts with VemP residues 36-60 and with SecD at position Asp-359. Loss of ppiD stabilizes the processed arrested form (AP-pro) and induces V.SecD2 expression. Genetic complementation shows non-redundant, cooperative function between PpiD and SecD/F.
results.evaluation: Claims C3, C5, C55, C75-C90, and C121-C122 provide strong convergent evidence through crosslinking (C55, C89-C90), genetic analysis (C75-C79, C84-C88), and functional studies (C5, C122). The differential accumulation of AP-pro vs AP-un forms between ppiD and ffh mutants (C80-C81) and the non-complementation experiments (C85-C87) demonstrate specific, non-redundant roles. Physical interaction between PpiD and SecD (C89-C90) supports the cooperative mechanism.

results.result: Arg-85 is a conserved residue that confers PpiD-dependence and regulates translocation-coupled arrest-cancelation. Mutations at Arg-85 destabilize arrest under secretion-proficient conditions but not under secretion-deficient conditions, indicating it acts during translocation rather than in establishing arrest per se. R85W mutation reduces PpiD-dependency of VemP translocation.
results.evaluation: Claims C6-C7, C91-C103, C106-C107, and C131-C133 demonstrate Arg-85's regulatory role through systematic mutagenesis (C91-C96), differential behavior under varying secretion conditions (C97-C98, C132-C133), and genetic epistasis with ppiD (C102-C103). The conservation data (C131) and mechanistic distinction from W143A (C98-C100) strengthen the conclusion. The convergence of mutational, functional, and evolutionary evidence supports this result.

results.result: VemP nascent chains interact sequentially with cellular factors during translocation. Crosslinking and kinetic analyses reveal that VemP interacts with uL22 and Ffh before engaging the translocon (SecY/SecG), and PpiD interaction occurs after translocon engagement. NaN3 treatment increases uL22/Ffh crosslinks while decreasing translocon/PpiD crosslinks.
results.evaluation: Claims C50-C59 and C63-C67 establish temporal ordering through kinetic crosslinking analysis (C57-C58, C66) and SecA inhibition experiments (C63-C65). The differential decay rates of crosslinks (C57-C58, C66) and opposite effects of NaN3 on early vs. late interactions (C63-C64) provide strong evidence for sequential engagement. The consistency with known protein localizations (C59, C67) validates the interpretation.

results.result: VemP monitors late steps in the protein translocation pathway. The arrest-cancelation occurs after signal sequence processing, involves SecD/F and PpiD which function at late translocation steps, and is proposed to monitor periplasmic motor activity of the Sec system.
results.evaluation: Claims C8, C38-C39, and C109-C115, C143 integrate prior knowledge (C38) with current findings to propose a comprehensive model. The observation that arrested VemP has processed signal sequences (C38-C39) combined with dependence on late-acting factors SecD/F and PpiD establishes that monitoring occurs post-signal cleavage. The proposed model (C109-C115, C143) is well-supported by the experimental data, though some mechanistic details remain speculative.

results.result: VemP uses the SRP pathway for co-translational targeting rather than the SecB-dependent post-translational pathway. SecA is required for early translocation steps, and its inhibition stabilizes the AP-un form. SecB deletion does not affect VemP arrest-cancelation but severely impairs MBP export.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C62 and C70-C71 demonstrate pathway specificity through complementary genetic approaches. The secA51(Ts) experiments (C62) confirm SecA requirement, while the differential effects of secB deletion on VemP vs. MBP (C70-C71) establish pathway distinction. The convergence of inhibitor studies (C60-C61) and genetic analysis provides strong support.

results.result: Arg-85 resides in the translocon-contacting region (residues 74-86) and acts as a translocation obstacle that requires PpiD/SecD/F-mediated force to overcome. When Arg-85 is mutated, translocation proceeds rapidly without significant arrest under secretion-proficient conditions, but arrest occurs normally under secretion-deficient conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C134-C142 propose a mechanistic model based on crosslinking data (C134-C135) and mutational analysis (C140-C141). The differential behavior under varying secretion conditions (C140-C141) and requirement for both SecA and PpiD/SecD/F forces (C142) support the obstacle model. However, some aspects remain speculative (C136, C139), and direct force measurements would strengthen the conclusion.

results.result: PpiD and SecD/F cooperate in arrest-cancelation through a proposed mechanism where PpiD captures emerging VemP and transfers it to the P1 head of SecD, which generates pulling force through conformational changes. PpiD itself does not generate pulling force as it is ATP-independent.
results.evaluation: Claims C116 and C123-C128 propose a mechanistic model that integrates known SecD/F motor function (C123) with observed PpiD-SecD interaction (C116). However, the substrate transfer mechanism (C126-C127) and prevention of reverse movement (C128) are speculative interpretations (evidence_type includes SPECULATION). While the model is plausible and consistent with available data, direct evidence for the proposed hand-off mechanism is lacking. In vitro reconstitution or additional structural studies would be needed to fully support this model.

results.result: Different monitoring substrates (VemP, SecM, MifM) employ distinct force-generation mechanisms to monitor different sub-steps of translocation. VemP monitors late steps via SecD/F and PpiD, while SecM monitors early steps via SecA. Cis-elements aid monitoring through different mechanisms in different substrates.
results.evaluation: Claims C144-C152 synthesize current findings with established knowledge about other monitoring substrates (C145-C147). The comparison between VemP and SecM mechanisms (C146-C149) is well-supported by cited literature and current data. The general conclusion about diverse force-sensing mechanisms (C144, C150-C152) is justified by the demonstrated differences in timing, factors involved, and cis-element functions. This represents a significant conceptual advance in understanding translational regulation.

results.result: Background knowledge about the Sec system, VemP regulation, and experimental methods. This includes the composition and function of the Sec translocon, SRP pathway, SecD/F motor, VemP's role in V.secD2/F2 regulation, PiXie methodology, and conservation of Sec machinery between Vibrio and E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claims C1, C9-C49, C117-C120, and C129 represent established knowledge from prior literature, supported by appropriate citations. These provide essential context for interpreting the current findings. The conservation between Vibrio and E. coli (C43-C49) justifies the use of E. coli as a heterologous system for studying VemP. All claims are well-documented in the cited literature.

results.result: PpiD has a general role in protein translocation beyond VemP. MBP translocation is retarded by ppiD disruption, and VemP(F.S.) lacking arrest motif shows PpiD-dependent translocation that is relieved by R85W mutation.
results.evaluation: Claims C76, C83, C104-C105 demonstrate that PpiD function extends beyond VemP-specific arrest-cancelation. The MBP data (C76) shows general translocation effects, while VemP(F.S.) experiments (C104-C105) separate arrest from translocation functions. The R85W effect on VemP(F.S.) (C105) confirms Arg-85's role in imposing PpiD-dependency independent of arrest. These findings support the broader significance of PpiD in Sec-mediated translocation.

results.result: W143A mutation abolishes arrest even in the absence of signal sequence, demonstrating that Trp-143 is part of the core arrest motif. This contrasts with Arg-85, which only affects arrest under secretion-proficient conditions.
results.evaluation: Claims C99-C100 establish the mechanistic distinction between W143A (arrest motif) and R85 (regulatory element) through experiments with signal sequence deletion. The differential behavior (C99) and explicit comparison (C100) are well-supported by the data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D. This distinction is important for understanding VemP's regulatory mechanism.

results.result: The cooperative function of SecD/F and PpiD could be utilized for late-step translocation of unidentified secretory proteins in organisms lacking VemP, given their conservation in enterobacteria including E. coli.
results.evaluation: Claim C130 is speculative (evidence_type: SPECULATION) and represents a hypothesis for future investigation rather than a demonstrated result. While the conservation of SecD/F and PpiD is established (C129), and their cooperative function in VemP translocation is demonstrated, the existence and identity of other substrates requiring this cooperation remains unknown. This represents a reasonable hypothesis but lacks experimental support.
